article.title: Why a Raise Can Feel Smaller Than Expected
article.framework: Nominal Raise → Inflation Adjustment → New Reference Point → Spending Adaptation → Real Gain
article.coreIdea: A higher salary is a nominal flow; whether it improves life depends on purchasing power, changing reference points, and how much of the increase becomes lasting saving rather than new spending.
article.body:
Imagine receiving an email that says your salary will rise by 8 percent next year. At first, the number feels substantial. You may picture better restaurants, more travel, or finally saving more each month. Yet several months later, the improvement can feel surprisingly small. Your bank account is not empty, but life does not seem 8 percent better. Where did the raise go?

The first answer is inflation. A salary is usually quoted in nominal terms: the number of dollars, pounds, or yuan you receive. What matters for living standards, however, is real income—what that money can actually buy. If your salary rises by 8 percent while the prices of the things you buy rise by 5 percent, your purchasing power has improved, but by much less than the headline raise suggests. The exact calculation is slightly different from simply subtracting five from eight, but the intuition is correct: part of the nominal increase merely compensates for higher prices.

This distinction between nominal and real values is fundamental in economics. It appears in wages, investment returns, interest rates, and economic growth. An investment that earns 6 percent during a period of 4 percent inflation has not increased your purchasing power by the full 6 percent. Similarly, a country can report rising nominal spending even when households are buying roughly the same quantity of goods. Whenever money values change over time, the first question should be: how much of the change is price, and how much is real?

But inflation is only part of the story. Even when a raise clearly increases real income, people often adapt their spending. A worker who once brought lunch from home may start buying it near the office. Taxis become easier to justify. A slightly more expensive apartment begins to feel reasonable. None of these decisions is necessarily irresponsible. The problem is that small upgrades can accumulate until much of the additional income has been absorbed into a new normal.

This process is often called lifestyle inflation or lifestyle creep. As income rises, spending rises with it, sometimes almost automatically. The mechanism is partly practical: higher-income jobs may require different clothes, commuting patterns, or social activities. But psychology also matters. What once felt like a luxury can gradually become a baseline expectation. After a few months of using a faster delivery service or living in a better neighborhood, returning to the old option may feel like a loss rather than a neutral return to the previous standard.

That is a reference-point effect. People do not judge outcomes only by their absolute level; they compare them with what they have become used to. This connects to loss aversion from earlier lessons. Suppose your monthly income rises by $500 and you immediately add $350 of recurring lifestyle expenses. You still have an extra $150 each month, so objectively you are better off. Yet after the new spending becomes normal, losing any of those upgrades can feel painful. The raise has improved consumption, but it has also moved the reference point.

There is another useful distinction here: stock versus flow. Salary is a flow—it arrives over a period of time. Wealth is a stock—the accumulated resources you own at a particular moment. A higher flow does not automatically create a much larger stock. If every extra dollar of income becomes an extra dollar of consumption, the person may earn far more without building much financial resilience. Two people with identical salaries can therefore have very different balance sheets depending on saving, debt, and existing assets.

This is why the destination of a raise matters as much as its size. Imagine two workers who each receive an extra $400 per month after tax. One automatically invests $250 and spends the remaining $150. The other adds several subscriptions, upgrades a car payment, and moves to a more expensive apartment. After a year, both have enjoyed a higher income, but their financial positions have changed in very different ways. The first has converted part of a temporary flow into an accumulating stock. The second has converted much of it into recurring obligations.

Recurring costs deserve special attention because they create second-order effects. A one-time $300 purchase costs $300. A $100 monthly upgrade costs $1,200 each year and may continue for years. It can also reduce flexibility: if income later falls, fixed commitments are harder to reverse than occasional spending. The first-order effect of a raise is obvious—more money arrives. The second-order effect depends on what new habits and obligations the higher income makes possible.

Taxes can further widen the gap between the raise people hear about and the money they feel. A company may announce a percentage increase in gross salary, but households make decisions with after-tax income. The relationship is not always simple because tax systems, deductions, and benefits differ. The broader analytical lesson is more important than any particular tax rule: identify the relevant measurement. If the question is “How much more can I spend or save?”, gross salary may be the wrong variable.

Comparison with other people can also weaken the emotional impact of higher income. A raise may feel impressive until colleagues receive larger ones, or until someone moves into a social environment where higher spending is normal. Relative income can affect satisfaction because people use peers as reference points. This does not mean only status matters; absolute resources clearly matter, especially when income is low. But once basic needs are secure, social comparison can influence whether an improvement feels large or small.

Companies understand some of these psychological effects. Compensation is not only a cost; it is also an incentive and a signal. A raise can communicate recognition, improve retention, or motivate effort. Yet its effect depends on expectations. An employee expecting a 10 percent increase may feel disappointed by 6 percent even though another employee would celebrate the same amount. As with markets, the outcome is evaluated against a benchmark. Good news can produce a negative reaction when the prior expectation was higher.

For individuals, the most useful response is not to avoid enjoying a raise. Money is partly valuable because it can improve life. The goal is to separate deliberate upgrades from automatic adaptation. One simple strategy is to decide where the additional income will go before it arrives. Some can improve current life, some can strengthen savings or investments, and some can remain flexible. By allocating the increase in advance, a person creates an incentive structure before new habits establish themselves.

Measurement helps too. Instead of asking only, “How much did my salary rise?”, ask several questions: How much did after-tax income rise? How much did prices rise? How much did recurring spending rise? How much did savings or net worth rise? These questions separate the headline number from the actual mechanism. They also prevent one attractive metric—salary—from becoming a substitute for the broader goal of financial well-being.

The deeper lesson is that income growth is not the same as wealth growth, and neither is identical to well-being. A raise can increase all three, but the connection is not automatic. Nominal income must survive inflation to become real purchasing power. Extra cash flow must avoid being fully absorbed by new expenses if it is to build wealth. And higher consumption must actually improve life rather than merely reset expectations.

So when the next raise arrives, the most useful question may not be “How much more am I earning?” It may be: “What part of this increase will still be improving my life a year from now?” That question shifts attention from the headline percentage to the lasting change—and from a temporary flow of money to the stock of choices it can create.
article.summaryZh:
这篇文章拆解了一个很常见的错觉：工资涨了 8%，生活为什么没有“变好 8%”？第一层是 nominal vs real。工资条上的涨幅只是名义变化；真正影响生活的是扣除价格上涨之后的 purchasing power。因此看到任何以货币表示的增长，都应该先问：其中多少来自价格，多少是真实数量或购买力的增加。

第二层是 lifestyle inflation。真实收入增加以后，人会逐渐升级消费，而升级后的生活方式又会成为新的 reference point。原本的“享受”会变成“正常”，以后取消它反而像一种损失。这把此前的 loss aversion 和 reference point 接到了个人财务上。

第三层是 stock vs flow。工资是 flow，财富是 stock。收入更高并不自动意味着财富积累更快，关键在于新增现金流最终流向消费、债务还是储蓄与投资。尤其需要警惕 recurring costs：一次性消费只发生一次，而新增月租、车贷或订阅会把今天的加薪转化为未来持续的固定义务。

文章最后把 measurement、expectations 和 second-order effects 串起来：不能只盯 headline salary，而应分别观察 after-tax income、inflation、recurring spending 和 net worth。今天的核心工具是“Flow-to-Stock Conversion”：面对任何资源增加，都问它有多少只是短期流量，有多少最终沉淀成长期能力、资产或选择权。

speaking.question: Why do some people fail to save more even after their income increases?
speaking.framework: Higher income → Lifestyle adaptation → Recurring costs → Limited wealth accumulation
speaking.response: I think one major reason is that spending often adapts to income. When people start earning more, some upgrades are reasonable, but they can gradually become part of the normal lifestyle. A nicer apartment, more convenient transport or several small subscriptions may not seem expensive individually, yet together they can absorb most of the extra income. I also think recurring costs matter more than people expect because they continue every month. So a higher salary does not automatically translate into greater financial security; what matters is how much of the additional cash flow is eventually converted into savings, investments or lower debt.
expressions: Small upgrades can gradually become part of the normal lifestyle.
A higher salary does not automatically translate into greater financial security.

speaking.question: Is salary the best way to judge whether someone is financially successful?
speaking.framework: Income flow → Assets and liabilities → Flexibility → Broader financial position
speaking.response: Not really. Salary is important because it determines how much money is coming in, but it only describes a flow of income. It tells us very little about a person's savings, debt, investments or fixed expenses. Someone with a high salary may still have little financial flexibility if most of that income is already committed, while someone earning less may have built substantial assets over time. I would therefore look at the broader financial position rather than one headline number. Income matters, but wealth and resilience show how many choices a person can actually afford to make.

I would look at the broader financial position rather than one headline number.
Wealth and resilience show how many choices a person can actually afford to make.
